title: Mentor a colleague to enhance the individual`s knowledge, skills, values and attitudes in a selected career path

lessons.title: What mentoring is and how to start
lessons.html:
Mentoring a colleague

A mentor is an experienced person who helps a less experienced colleague grow in their career. On a farm or in an extension office, this could be a senior extension officer guiding a new graduate, or an experienced supervisor helping a newly promoted team leader in the packhouse. Mentoring is different from training. Training teaches a set skill in a set time. Mentoring is a longer relationship that builds knowledge, skills, values and attitudes over months.

Roles of a mentor

  • Guide: shares experience about the job and the career path.
  • Coach: helps the mentee practise skills and gives feedback.
  • Role model: shows good values such as honesty, punctuality and respect for farmers.
  • Connector: introduces the mentee to useful people, for example a commodity organisation contact or a veterinary official.

Starting the relationship

Hold a first meeting in a quiet place. Get to know each other. Ask the mentee about their background, what they enjoy, and where they want to be in three to five years. A young extension officer may want to specialise in livestock, or move into project management.

Agree on the basics and write them down:

  1. How often you will meet, for example every two weeks for one hour.
  2. Where you will meet: in the office, in the bakkie on the way to farm visits, or in the field.
  3. What is confidential between you.
  4. How long the mentoring will last, for example six months, with a review at the end.

Be honest about your own limits. You do not need to know everything. If the mentee needs knowledge you do not have, help them find another expert.

Remember that the mentee owns their development. Your job is to support and challenge, not to make every decision for them.

lessons.title: Setting goals and building a development plan
lessons.html:
Assessing where the mentee is now

Before setting goals, find out what the mentee already knows and can do. Use their job description, any performance review, and your own observation. Look at four areas:

AreaExample for a new extension officer
KnowledgeUnderstands crop rotation, soil sampling and livestock diseases
SkillsRuns a farmer day, writes a report, uses a GPS
ValuesTreats all farmers fairly, keeps promises, respects culture
AttitudesWilling to learn, patient, positive about rural work

Ask the mentee to rate themselves, then share your view. Talk about the gaps openly and kindly.

Writing SMART goals

Help the mentee write goals that are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. A weak goal is: get better at farmer days. A SMART goal is: plan and run one farmer day on maize planting for the Ward 7 farmers by the end of March, with at least 20 farmers attending and a short feedback form.

The development plan

Put the goals into a simple plan with:

  • The goal.
  • Activities to reach it, such as shadowing you on farm visits, reading a guide, or attending a short course.
  • Resources needed, such as transport or a budget for a course.
  • A target date.
  • How progress will be shown, for example a report you can review.

Keep the plan realistic. Three or four goals at a time are enough. The mentee should sign the plan and keep a copy. Link the plan to their career path, so that each step brings them closer to the role they want.

lessons.title: Running mentoring sessions and reviewing progress
lessons.html:
Good mentoring sessions

Each session should have a purpose. Start by asking what has happened since the last meeting. Look at progress on the plan. Then talk about a challenge the mentee is facing, such as a farmer who does not follow advice or a difficult supervisor.

Skills a mentor uses

  • Active listening: give full attention, do not interrupt, and repeat back what you heard.
  • Open questions: ask what, how and why questions, such as: what options do you have? This helps the mentee think for themselves.
  • Demonstration: show a skill, then let the mentee try it while you watch. For example, you lead the first part of a soil sampling visit and the mentee does the next part.
  • Feedback: be specific, describe the behaviour not the person, and say what went well before what to improve.

Handling problems

Sometimes the mentee misses meetings or does not complete tasks. Talk about it early and calmly. Find out the reason. There may be personal problems, transport issues or too much work. Adjust the plan if needed. If there are serious issues such as safety or misconduct, follow your organisation's procedures and involve the manager.

Reviewing and closing

Every month or two, review the plan together. Tick off goals that are met and celebrate them. Set new goals where needed. Keep short notes of each session, with dates and agreed actions.

At the end of the agreed period, hold a closing meeting. Look back at what the mentee has learnt and how they have grown. Ask for feedback on your mentoring too, so you can improve. The relationship may continue informally, but the formal programme should have a clear end.

Key points

  • Mentoring builds knowledge, skills, values and attitudes over a longer period.
  • Agree on meeting times, confidentiality and duration at the start.
  • Assess the mentee's current level and write SMART goals in a development plan.
  • Use active listening, open questions, demonstration and specific feedback.
  • Review progress regularly and close the programme with a formal review.
